title: No limits. True mettā (loving-kindness) has no lim (p. 46–60)
html:
Ten Perfections · Children’s Books

No limits. True mettā (loving-kindness) has no lim (p. 46–60)

Pages 46–60 (15 pages)
Page 46

No limits. True mettā (loving-kindness) has no limits. If it is kept for some people and not others, it may not be mettā (loving-kindness) at all, but lobha (attachment12), which only looks like kindness from the outside. The test is this: if there is true mettā (loving-kindness), a kind deed13 for a stranger feels exactly the same as a kind deed for someone close. A mother and her child. The Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets) compares deeds done with mettā (lovingkindness) to a mother’s care for her child. She gives up everything for the child, and looks after it even when it is dirty. But there is a warning. A mother’s attachment to her own child is not mettā (lovingkindness). The picture is of her selfless care. A person who can care for other people the way a good mother cares for her baby practises mettā (loving-kindness). The woman in Indonesia. A monk14 told of a woman in Indonesia whose husband was killed by a young man’s reckless15 driving. She did not take him to court, because she did not want to cause unhappiness to anyone. More than that, she said she would pay for the young man’s education. The book says this was very hard for her, and she did it. Such acts can be done by someone who has built up loving-kindness and compassion16 over a long time. Anger lasts one moment. When anger arises towards someone, it helps to know that anger arises only for a moment and then falls away17, and that mettā (loving-kindness) can arise in its place. A person who stays angry for a long time can see from that how much is still to be done. The four divine abidings. Mettā (loving-kindness) is one of four brahmavihāra (divine abidings): 1. Mettā (loving-kindness): wishing beings well. 2. Karuṇā (compassion): wishing to take away a being’s suffering18. 3. Muditā (sympathetic joy19): being glad at another’s happiness and success. 4. Upekkhā (equanimity20): being even-minded21 towards all beings, with neither attachment nor aversion. The Atthasālinī (The Expositor) gives a picture of four children. Mettā (loving-kindness) is like the care for a small child, whom everyone wishes to grow up well. Karuṇā (compassion) is like the care for a sick child, whom the mother wants to see cured. Muditā (sympathetic joy) is like the gladness of parents whose child is growing up well. Upekkhā (equanimity) is like the calm of parents whose child can now manage his own affairs. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 46

Page 47

mettā loving-kindness a small child whom everyone wishes to grow up well karuṇā compassion a sick child whom the mother wants to see cured muditā sympathetic joy a child growing up well the gladness of the parents upekkhā equanimity a grown child who manages his own affairs “Mettā is like a small child, compassion is like a child who is sick, sympathetic joy is like a child who is becoming an adolescent and equanimity is like a child who manages his own affairs.” Look-alikes. Each of the four has a near enemy, a state that looks like it but is akusala (bad). When a person is thrilled by someone else’s gain and praise, there may be lobha (attachment), not muditā (sympathetic joy). The near enemy of upekkhā (equanimity) is plain indifference22. When something is seen and there is no reaction, that is not always kusala (good). It may be moha (ignorance23). Only paññā (wisdom) can tell them apart. Kindness at the right time. When people see someone doing a harmful deed, they are upset and hope he will get what he deserves. When later he suffers the result24, they feel sorry for him. That is the wrong way round. The moment for mettā (loving-kindness) and karuṇā (compassion) is the moment he does the deed, because that deed is the cause of his future suffering. “If one sympathizes25 with him when he receives an undesirable result, one sympathizes too late.” A real friend helps a person to give up bad deeds. No persons. In the ultimate26 sense there are no beings and no persons; there are only realities arising and falling away. A person who lives by the Dhamma (the teaching) comes to know at once when there is no loving-kindness but akusala (bad states), and can then have loving-kindness at once, even for a person who behaves like an enemy. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 2. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 3. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 4. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 5. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 6. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 7. resentment: a sore, angry feeling about being treated badly 8. kindliness: kindness 9. determination: making up one's mind firmly and keeping to it 10. unshakeable: cannot be shaken or moved 11. conceit: thinking oneself better than others, or worse, or just as good; pride that compares 12. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 13. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 14. monk: a man who has left home to follow the Buddha's rule of life 15. recklessness: doing things without care for what may happen The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 47

16. compassion: wanting to help someone who is suffering 17. fall away: to end; to stop; to be gone 18. suffering: pain and trouble; anything that cannot give lasting happiness 19. sympathetic joy: being glad when someone else is happy or does well 20. equanimity: an even, calm mind that is not shaken by good luck or bad 21. even-mindedness: having a mind that stays level and calm whatever happens 22. indifferent: neither pleasant nor unpleasant; in the middle 23. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 24. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 25. sympathize: to feel for someone; to share their feelings 26. ultimate: the deepest and most real; what is really there when all the names are taken away The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 48

Chapter 10. Upekkhā (even-mindedness) “I slept in a cemetery, taking as a pillow the skeleton of a corpse. I had evenmindedness with regard to what is clean and what is dirty.” Upekkhā (even-mindedness1) is not being disturbed by the troublesome conduct of people, or by the ups and downs of life, pleasant or unpleasant: gain and loss, praise and blame. The book compares it to a pair of scales that is well balanced. Upekkhā (even-mindedness) What it is taking a neutral2 stance towards beings3 What it does sees things impartially4 How it shows itself the dying down of attraction and repulsion5 What it needs the thought that all beings inherit the results6 of their own kamma (deeds7) The snake and the man who kills it. When people see someone kill a snake, they believe they feel compassion8 for the snake. In reality9, the book says, they are disturbed by aversion10 towards the person who kills it. There may not be loving-kindness11 at all. But there can be upekkhā (even-mindedness) when it is remembered that everyone receives the results of his own deeds. And there can be compassion for the killer, who will receive the result of what he does. A person with upekkhā (even-mindedness) is not disturbed, and does not say unsuitable things to someone doing wrong. A disturbed citta (consciousness12) is akusala (bad), even when it feels righteous. No expectations. A person should not have expectations about when the four noble truths will be seen. As long as many kilesa (defilements13) arise14 all the time, the goal is far away. The thing to do is to develop every kind of good, patiently, so that the conditions15 are slowly built up. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 49

Page 50

Each perfection is the enemy of attachment. The commentary16 explains how each of the ten perfections17 works against lobha (attachment18), dosa (anger) and moha (ignorance19). Giving works against them because there is no attachment to the gift, no hate towards the one who receives it, and no ignorance about the result. The book gives an example. A person sees a beggar and notices that he is strong, or sees that he drags a disabled child along, and feels irritated, and so does not give. At that moment there is aversion towards the receiver, and no giving. Wisdom works against them because they make a person blind and wisdom gives back sight. Patience works against lobha (attachment) “by accepting the desirable, the undesirable, and emptiness”. And upekkhā (even-mindedness) works against them by driving out attraction to pleasant things and repulsion from unpleasant ones, and by going on evenly whatever happens. A thousand goods on the doorstep. An ancient commentary compares the Buddha’s teaching to a thousand goods laid down on the doorstep of every house, for the family inside. Some people open the door and take them in. Others never open the door. Another passage compares people’s confusion about cause and result to a cotton thread so tangled into a knot that nobody can undo it alone. Only two kinds of person can undo it: a Sammāsambuddha (a fully enlightened20 Buddha who teaches the world) and a Paccekabuddha (a silent Buddha, who finds the truth alone but does not teach it). Lomahaṃsa, who slept among the bones. The Cariyāpiṭaka (Basket of Conduct) calls this the Great Astounding Conduct. It is the life in which the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) developed upekkhā (evenmindedness) to the highest degree. gain, praise, honour, happiness flowers, scented oils and food loss, blame, dishonour, misery spitting, jeering, grass in the ears upekkhā (even-mindedness) "I am impartial towards everything, and this is my perfection of equanimity." “The perfection of equanimity is evenmindedness, being without happiness and anguish, like a scale that is wellbalanced.” He was born into a wealthy family. When his parents died, his relatives begged him to take charge of the family’s wealth. But he had thought about impermanence21, and he felt saṃvega (urgency22). He thought of becoming a monk23. Then he reflected that a monk receives honour and gifts, and he did not want honour or gain. So he decided to live with just enough, as a layman24, and to be even-minded in gain and loss and the other ups and downs of the world. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 50

Page 51

He resolved: “I shall accumulate25 the practice of supreme patience, enduring26 derisive27 speech from others. I shall develop the perfection of equanimity28 to the highest degree.” He left home in the clothes he was wearing. Though he was not dumb, he behaved as if he were dumb, and people mocked him because he looked like a fool. He wandered from village to village, staying one night in each place, and where he was mocked the most, he stayed longer. When his clothes wore out he went about in a rag. In one village he met a gang of children who were cruel and violent, and threw dust over the backs of the old and poor. He thought: here is a chance to develop the perfection of even-mindedness, and he stayed. When the children began to torment29 him, he pretended to be afraid, so that they would follow him. He led them to the cemetery30, lay down, and took a skeleton for a pillow. The children spat on him, poked grass into his ears and jeered, day after day. Wise people who saw it told the children to stop, and honoured him with flowers, scented oils and food. The Buddha said of that life: “I slept in a cemetery, taking as a pillow the skeleton of a corpse31. I had evenmindedness with regard to what is clean and what is dirty.” The children made him suffer, the wise people gave him pleasant things; he was even-minded to all of them. He had no special affection for those who helped him, and no angry words or thoughts of revenge for those who did not. “I am evenminded towards happiness and misery, towards honour and dishonour32; I am impartial towards everything, and this is my perfection of equanimity.” The commentary adds that in that same life he developed all ten perfections. He was not a monk, but he was a monk at heart, and his life was like the life of an arahant (a fully enlightened person). All ten. The book ends with the list once more: dāna (giving), sīla (good conduct), nekkhamma (letting go), paññā (wisdom), viriya (energy33), khanti (patience), sacca (truthfulness34), adhiṭṭhāna (determination35), mettā (loving-kindness) and upekkhā (even-mindedness). None of them should be left out. All of them are needed, and developing them is the way to develop paññā (wisdom). HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. even-mindedness: having a mind that stays level and calm whatever happens 2. neutral: neither one thing nor the other; in the middle 3. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 4. impartial: fair to all sides; not taking sides 5. repulsion: strong dislike; being pushed away 6. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 7. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 8. compassion: wanting to help someone who is suffering 9. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 10. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 11. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 12. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 13. defilement: something that makes the mind dirty: wanting, anger, not knowing and the rest 14. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 15. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 16. commentary: an old explanation of a text, written to make it clear 17. perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be 18. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 19. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 20. enlightenment: the moment when the truth is seen fully and for good, and the dirt of the mind is cut away 21. impermanent: not lasting; passing away The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 51

Quiz 5 (chapters 9 and 10) The answers are at the back. 1. In the Abhidhamma, mettā (loving-kindness) is which cetasika (mental factor)? (a) lobha (attachment) (b) adosa (non-hate) (c) viriya (energy) (d) saññā (memory) 2. What is the book’s test for finding out whether kindness is true mettā (loving-kindness) or only lobha (attachment)? 3. What did the woman in Indonesia do after her husband was killed by a reckless young driver? 4. The four brahmavihāra (divine abidings) are compared to four children. Put the four in the order the ancient texts give. muditā (sympathetic joy): a child growing up well karuṇā (compassion): a sick child mettā (loving-kindness): a small child upekkhā (equanimity): a child who manages his own affairs 5. According to the book, when is the right moment to feel mettā (loving-kindness) and karuṇā (compassion) for a person who does a harmful deed? (a) only after he has been punished (b) at the moment he does the deed, because that deed is the cause of his future suffering (c) never, because he deserves what he gets (d) only if he says sorry 6. When people see someone kill a snake, what do they think they feel, and what does the book say is really there? 7. What is the thousand goods on the doorstep, and what are the two kinds of people? 8. Why did Lomahaṃsa decide not to become a monk? (a) because he was too poor (b) because a monk receives honour and gifts, and he did not want honour or gain (c) because he did not believe the teaching (d) because his parents forbade it 9. What did Lomahaṃsa use as a pillow, and what did the Buddha say about his mind at that time? 10. True or false: the book says that when something is seen and there is no reaction at all, that is always upekkhā (even-mindedness) and always good. 11. What is the defilement of the perfection of sīla (good conduct), according to the commentary? Give one of the two examples in the book. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 53

Page 54

The defilements of the perfections The book ends with a short chapter on what makes each perfection imperfect. The commentary calls this the kilesa (defilement) of the perfections. The rule is simple: “When attachment arises, when we have enjoyment and clinging, the ten perfections are defiled.” What makes each one imperfect is a thought that picks and chooses where there should be no picking and choosing. Perfection What makes it imperfect dāna (giving) picking and choosing over gifts and over who receives them sīla (good conduct) picking and choosing over which people and which days the rules are kept for nekkhamma (letting go) delighting in sense pleasures and in being born again paññā (wisdom) thoughts of “I” and “mine”, even the thought “my wisdom” viriya (energy) leaning towards laziness or towards restlessness khanti (patience) thoughts of oneself and of others sacca (truthfulness) claiming to have seen what was not seen adhiṭṭhāna (determination) seeing faults in the things that lead to enlightenment, and good in their opposites mettā (loving-kindness) confusing what is harmful with what is helpful upekkhā (evenmindedness) picking and choosing between the pleasant and the unpleasant The book gives two examples for sīla (good conduct). Some people keep the rules of respect towards particular persons, such as their parents, but not towards other people. Some keep the rules only on the Uposatha (observance) day, the full-moon and new-moon days, and think they are perfect in conduct, although on the other days they do not keep them. And for upekkhā (even-mindedness) she notes that a person may be even-minded about the unpleasant but not about the pleasant. The last words of the book are these. The more the Dhamma (the teaching) is understood, the more a person will want to practise it. The perfections may have seemed beyond reach. But if the benefit of each one is seen, and they are developed little by little, they will in the end be accomplished. Listening to the Dhamma and studying it is of the greatest benefit, because it makes it possible to apply the Dhamma in daily life, and to develop satipaṭṭhāna (mindfulness of realities) together with all ten perfections. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 54

Hard words Every hard English word in this book has a small number after it the first time it is met in a chapter, and its meaning is given at the end of that chapter. Here are all of them together, in alphabetical order. abuse: to treat or speak to someone cruelly and rudely accumulate: to gather up bit by bit, so that there is more and more of it aeon: a huge stretch of time, far longer than anyone can count agony: very great pain arise: to come up; to begin; to happen ascetic: a person who gives up home and comfort to live simply and seek the truth; or that hard way of living aspire: to want very much to reach something high attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little awareness: noticing what is really there right now; another word for mindfulness being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being benefactor: a person who gives help or money brahmin: a man of the priestly class in ancient India cemetery: a place where the dead are buried or left censure: blame; telling someone off cessation: stopping; coming to an end chariot: a cart with two wheels pulled by horses, used in old times for war and travel charioteer: the driver of a chariot clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go coarse: rough; not fine commentary: an old explanation of a text, written to make it clear compassion: wanting to help someone who is suffering conceit: thinking oneself better than others, or worse, or just as good; pride that compares conch: a big sea shell that is blown like a trumpet condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing conventional: the ordinary everyday way of talking, as when a pile of parts is called a chariot corpse: a dead body council: a big meeting of the elder monks to settle something counsellor: a person who gives advice to a king courtier: a person who serves at a king’s court deceive: to fool someone;
